# Metashields
The [bold]Metashield[/bold] defines what your character may know at the start of a round, and what information must be learned in-character.
On Project Verdant, most threats, organizations, and strange phenomena are known to exist in some form. However, knowing that something exists does not mean your character knows how it works, how to identify it perfectly, how to counter it, or what secret equipment or abilities it may have.
The guiding rule is simple:
- [bold]Existence may be common knowledge.[/bold] - [bold]Detailed methods, counters, abilities, identities, and secret mechanics are not automatically known.[/bold] - Information learned through OOC knowledge, game mechanics, guidebooks, observing, ghosting, previous lives, previous rounds, or another character is not valid IC knowledge.
## Common Sense Clause
If your role, job, background, species, or antagonist role directly gives you access to something, you know what you need to know to use it.
Examples: - Traitors know how their uplink items work. - Thieves know how to use their special tools and know what their theft objectives are. - Nuclear Operatives know their own equipment and mission. - Shadekin know normal Shadekin knowledge. - A character who directly witnesses something may know what they witnessed, but not necessarily everything about it. - A character may recognize a visible threat without knowing hidden mechanics behind it.
## Meta Information
Meta information is never known IC unless learned in-character.
This includes: - The current gamemode. - Possible antagonists in the round. - Previous round hidden roles. - Information learned while dead, observing, or ghosting. - Information from Discord, streams, adminhelps, or other OOC communication. - Player habits or player identity. - Secret item functions revealed by game mechanics.
Examples: - You may not assume someone is an antagonist because of the round type. - You may not assume someone is an antagonist because the player usually plays Security. - You may not use right-click or examine text to discover hidden item functions unless the item explicitly gives valid IC information. - You may not know that an item is Syndicate equipment just because the game or guidebook tells you, unless your character has valid IC reason to know.
## Public Knowledge and Restricted Details
Most major threats are known to exist. However, the details of how they work are usually restricted, inaccurate, misunderstood, or not believed by the general public.
Knowing that something exists is not the same as knowing how to identify it, counter it, prove it, or explain it.
### Romerol
The existence of Romerol is common knowledge. A character may choose to know that Romerol exists.
Common crew do not know how Romerol works, how it spreads in detail, or how to effectively counter it.
Characters with the Romerol Disaster Survivor background know about Ambuzol and know how to effectively kill zombies.
### Abductors
The existence of Abductors is common knowledge.
Most people believe Abductors only target small, isolated groups or individuals, and that a staffed station is generally safe from them.
Their technology, methods, equipment, and true capabilities are not common knowledge.
### Ninjas
The Spider Clan is known to exist.
Most people believe they do not attack openly or target entire stations without reason.
Their technology is not common knowledge. This includes their cloaking, teleportation, and other advanced equipment.
### Paradox Clones
Paradox clones are considered a myth or theoretical possibility.
The fact that they actually exist is not widely known.
### Cults
Cults with real supernatural power, such as the Cosmic Cult, are not common knowledge.
They are secretive groups. Command may know of their possible existence, but must keep the identity and nature of the cult hidden while dealing with it unless disclosure becomes absolutely necessary.
Crew may know that normal cults, religions, and fringe groups exist, but not the details of cults with real power.
### Nuclear Operatives
Nuclear Operatives are common knowledge. People are aware that the Syndicate has Nuclear Operatives.
Most crew believe smaller stations are not meaningful targets and are unlikely to be attacked.
Command knows that Nuclear Operatives are a real threat even to smaller stations.
### Exterminators
Exterminators are known only to Central Command.
Their existence, origin, purpose, and capabilities are not common knowledge.
### Death Squad and Code Epsilon
Death Squads and Code Epsilon are not known to the public.
There may be rumors about Death Squads, but these are only rumors. Their actual existence is known only to Central Command members.
Code Epsilon is not known outside Central Command.
### Revolutionary Methods and Mind Control
People are aware of USSP revolutionary movements and that they use some form of mind control.
The method is not common knowledge.
Security Command and Central Command know how revolutionary mind control is commonly performed.
A normal crew member might believe revolutionaries use propaganda, media, interrogation, or private indoctrination, but they do not know the exact method unless they learn it IC.
### Bright-eyes
Bright-eyes are common knowledge.
Common crew do not know their abilities in detail.
Shadekin may know Bright-eyes in depth. Command and Central Command may know their abilities and threat profile.
### Suspected Syndicate Corporations
Suspected Syndicate-linked corporations are known as rumors, suspicions, and grey-zone information.
No official public statement has fully confirmed or denied these connections.
Characters may treat these corporations with suspicion, but should not treat rumor as hard proof without evidence.
### Non-NanoTrasen / TSF Implants
Non-NanoTrasen and non-TSF implants are known to exist.
Common crew do not know what these implants look like, what each implant does, or how to identify them reliably.
Security, Command, and Central Command may know more about implant types and their risks.
A character may not assume someone has an implant without valid evidence.
### Vampires
Vampires are common knowledge.
Most people believe vampires avoid stations and remain hidden in isolated places. Most public knowledge is based on stories, folklore, rumors, and inaccurate media.
Common crew do not know the full truth of vampire abilities or how they work.
### Wizards
Wizards and magic are common knowledge.
People know magic exists, but not how it works.
The detailed methods, limits, and mechanics of magic are secret knowledge held by wizard organizations and those directly involved.
### Xenoborgs
Xenoborgs are hidden knowledge.
Command and Central Command know of Xenoborgs.
Security may be briefed on Xenoborgs if necessary.
The common crew should not be told the full truth unless absolutely necessary. If public explanation is required, they should generally be described as faulty, rogue, or malfunctioning borgs unless the situation demands a more complete disclosure.
## Syndicate Equipment
Syndicate equipment is not common knowledge.
Most crew would not know that an item is Syndicate equipment just by seeing it.
A character may recognize obvious weapons, suspicious equipment, or well-known items if it makes sense for their background or role. For example, someone may recognize a suspicious weapon or a Cybersun-branded pen.
However, secret equipment such as hypopens, energy daggers, chameleon items, and other hidden-use tools are not known unless the character has valid IC knowledge.
Right-clicking, examining, or using game mechanics to identify a hidden Syndicate item or its secret function is forbidden unless the item explicitly provides IC-visible information or your character has valid IC knowledge.
Characters who know what an item is may act on that knowledge. Characters who do not know what it is may only react to what they can reasonably observe.
## High-Value Theft Targets
Some high-value items are common sense targets. Crew may understand that important command, research, security, or engineering equipment is valuable.
However, these items should not be hidden or protected in a way that prevents antagonist or thief gameplay without strong IC reason.
Examples of forbidden or poor handling: - Hiding the nuclear authentication disk inside a plushie. - Hiding the spare Captain ID inside random clothing. - Moving theft targets to obscure locations solely to deny thieves their objectives.
The Captain's spare ID may remain in the Captain's locker or be issued when needed, but it should not be hidden away only to prevent theft.
Important items may be secured reasonably, but should remain accessible through normal roleplay, escalation, investigation, theft, or conflict.
## Background Knowledge
A character background may allow specific additional knowledge.
Examples: - Romerol Disaster Survivors may know Ambuzol and effective anti-zombie methods. - Shadekin may know more about Bright-eyes. - Former soldiers or criminals may know some weapons, theft targets, or black-market concepts. - Characters with direct past experiences may know more about a specific threat, but only within the limits of that background.
Backgrounds should not be used to justify knowing everything about a threat, item, antagonist, or secret organization.
## Revealing Restricted Knowledge
Restricted information may be revealed when necessary to preserve lives, resolve a crisis, or respond to a confirmed threat.
When possible, reveal only what is needed.
Examples: - Command may warn crew about a threat without explaining every hidden detail. - Security may brief officers on a threat without publicly revealing sensitive information. - Medical may be told how to treat a specific condition without being told unrelated classified details. - Crew may be warned to avoid an area without being told the full nature of the threat.
## Metafriending and Metagrudging
Giving a character preferential treatment because of OOC knowledge is metafriending.
Treating a character negatively because of OOC knowledge is metagrudging.
This includes knowledge from: - Player identity. - Previous rounds. - Previous lives. - Discord or other OOC communication. - Knowing someone's usual role or usual antagonist behavior.
Characters may build relationships over multiple rounds, but they may not use those relationships to ignore objectives, bypass roleplay, or act on information their current character does not reasonably know.
### Knowledge of Past Shifts
Characters may remember limited events from past shifts, but only as ordinary memories of what they personally experienced or what was publicly known during that shift.
This rule exists to support ongoing character relationships, reputations, distrust, rumors, trauma, and dynamic roleplay. It does not allow players to carry over antagonist knowledge, hidden roles, secret mechanics, or exact round information.
The guiding rule is:
- You may remember what your character personally witnessed or experienced. - You may remember the broad outcome of major public events. - You may remember that someone committed a visible crime or harmful act if your character personally witnessed or experienced it. - You may not remember, claim, imply, or act on knowledge of what hidden role someone had. - You may not remember, claim, imply, or act on knowledge of what hidden role you yourself had in a past shift. - You may not remember secret mechanics, antagonist objectives, antagonist equipment details, or hidden round information. - You may not use past-shift knowledge to ruin roleplay, deny gameplay, or punish another player.
Past-shift memory only goes as far as observable actions and public events.
Examples: - Allowed: "X assaulted me last shift." - Allowed: "X stole from my department last shift." - Allowed: "X acted suspiciously around the vault last shift." - Allowed: "I do not fully trust X because of what they did before." - Allowed: "There was an outbreak last shift." - Allowed: "There was a major explosion last shift." - Allowed: "Some borgs went rogue last shift." - Not allowed: "X was a Syndicate agent last shift." - Not allowed: "X was a thief last shift." - Not allowed: "X was an antagonist last shift." - Not allowed: "I was a Syndicate agent last shift." - Not allowed: "I know how this antagonist works because I was one last shift." - Not allowed: attacking someone because they killed you last shift. - Not allowed: refusing to treat, hire, serve, or cooperate with someone only because of a past-shift conflict. - Not allowed: using past-shift suspicion as a replacement for current-shift evidence.
For major threats: - Romerol may be remembered as a past outbreak or infected incident if it was witnessed or publicly known. - Wizard encounters may be remembered as strange magical events if witnessed or publicly known. - Nuclear Operative rounds may be remembered by most crew only as major destruction, disaster, explosion, evacuation, or an unknown attack, not confirmed Nuclear Operatives. - Xenoborg attacks may be remembered by most crew only as rogue, faulty, or malfunctioning borg incidents, not confirmed Xenoborgs.
This rule is meant to enhance roleplay, not restrict it. Characters may develop memories, relationships, fears, distrust, and reputations over time, but those memories should create roleplay opportunities rather than shut down gameplay.
